children: 1017 GMT - The 1.1% drop in German industrial output in July defies the solid order intake and noticeable recent improvement in business sentiment, KfW chief economist Dirk Schumacher says. "The decline in industrial production can therefore be explained primarily by production changes in the automotive industry," he says. German data agency Destatis noted that a multi-week shutdown at a car plant was likely one of the main drivers of the fall. In August and September, the low water levels of the Rhine likely further dampened production, Schumacher says. However, the signals from orders and sentiment indicators point to the underlying improving trend, even if that will probably only be reflected in the figures for the fourth quarter, he says. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

1004 GMT - The AfD landslide in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt will pile further pressure on the national government in Berlin and on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's leadership, Commerzbank's Ralph Solveen says in a note. Moreover, the poor showing by the Christian Democrats and Social Democrats is likely to strain the coalition's cooperation and make it no easier to reach agreements on upcoming reforms, he says. However, an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt won't impact policy areas of greatest interest to financial markets--taxes, social security, and the makeup of the labor market. The AfD promises to advocate for its chosen issues in the federal upper house--the Bundesrat--though it remains ostracized from the mainstream parties, Solveen says. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0957 GMT - A fragile and uncertain geopolitical backdrop, with oil prices rising due to renewed hostilities in the Middle East, should sustain demand for the U.S. dollar as a safe-haven asset, Eleonex CEO Stefan Arsenovic says in a note. Persistent tensions in the Middle East also sustain inflation concerns and reinforcing the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, he says. The dollar falls on Monday, for now shrugging off higher oil prices in thin trade due to a U.S. public holiday and helped by gains in the Japanese yen. This week's input for the dollar could come from producer prices on Thursday and consumer prices on Friday. The DXY dollar index falls 0.2% to 98.953. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0930 GMT - The recent rise in German Bund yields reflects expectations of higher eurozone interest rates rather than demand for compensation for buying longer-dated debt, Generali Investments' Florian Spaete says in a note. The 10-year Bund yield's increase of close to 50 basis points in the third quarter to a 15-year high was "driven almost entirely by a repricing of European Central Bank rate expectations," the strategist says. Markets fully price a 25-basis-point hike in September and nearly two more by summer 2027, yet the 10-year Bund term premium has barely moved since late June, he says. The term premium, around 0.5%, is still low by historical standards, suggesting that the recent yield rise is mostly a policy-rate story, he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0929 GMT - The cost of insuring euro-denominated credit against default climbs as risk appetite weakens after the U.S. and Iran resumed hostilities over the weekend. The U.S. said it struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran launched attacks toward two Navy warships. The iTraxx Europe Crossover index of euro high-yield credit default swaps rises 1 basis point to 250bps, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0841 GMT - An interest-rate hike by the European Central Bank on Thursday "looks all but locked in," Amundi Investment Institute's Alessia Berardi says in a note. After that, Amundi expects the ECB to stay on hold in the remainder of the year. "We do not see further hikes in 2026 but are watching renewed upside risks from gas and food which could make inflation more entrenched and start to feed second-round effects that are not yet visible," the head of global macroeconomics says. Inflation remains elevated and should stay sticky over the next few months before easing toward the second half of next year, while growth risks and pressure in sovereign yields could keep it from moving too aggressively, Berardi says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0815 GMT - Gilt investors' focus is on U.K. Treasury Chief John Healey's speech due at 0830 GMT as government borrowing costs climb. Healey is expected to reassure markets about the government's spending plans ahead of the budget on October 28, Mizuho's Evelyne Gomez-Liechti says in a note. "Better growth rhetoric may help at the margin, but markets will care more about whether the numbers preserve fiscal credibility." Ten-year gilt yields rise 1.2 basis points to last trade at 5.151%, Tradeweb data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0806 GMT - Singapore's retail sales momentum is likely to moderate through 2026, RHB Bank's Barnabas Gan says in a report. Retail sales grew by 1.5% on year in July, compared to 4.0% in June. Rising geopolitical uncertainty, particularly in the Middle East, could weigh on consumer and business confidence. This would encourage more cautious spending and moderating discretionary demand, Gan says. Tourism-dependent segments, including luxury retail, department stores and jewelry, also face more headwinds if there are fewer visitors in Singapore or softening tourist spending. RHB maintains its 2026 retail sales growth for Singapore at 3.0%. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0758 GMT - A win for Germany's far-right AfD party in a regional election is unlikely to impede economic reform, Holger Schmieding at Berenberg says in a note. The AfD's support more than doubled in the Saxony-Anhalt election, while chancellor Friedrich Merz's vote share tumbled. "The unpopularity of Merz and concerns about the pension and other reforms which his government is planning to raise Germany's growth potential played a significant role," Schmieding says. However, Merz and his coalition government will likely continue until the end of their term in early 2029, he adds. And while planned pro-growth reforms may be softened at the margins, the bulk should still be passed this autumn. "The planned increases in defense and infrastructure spending should also not be affected." (don.forbes@wsj.com)

0749 GMT - China's inflation data is likely to be mixed in August, according to Deutsche Bank economists in a research note. The bank expects China's PPI inflation to moderate to 3.2% on year in August from 3.5% in July, DB says. "While the rebound in oil prices over the past two months continued to support price gains in the petroleum sector, price trends across most other industries were largely flat," the bank says. By contrast, DB expects CPI inflation to pick up to 0.8% on year from 0.5%, driven by continued increases in pork and vegetable prices. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0735 GMT - Gold prices fall after surprisingly strong U.S. jobs data and renewed Middle East tensions reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise rates next week. In early European trading, New York futures are down 0.8% to $4,442.40 a troy ounce. "Gold has remained volatile around $4,400 after recovering from July lows near $4,000 an ounce," says Soojin Kim from MUFG. "This week's U.S. inflation data will be critical in determining whether the Fed tightens policy at its Sept. 15-16 meeting, with persistent price pressures likely to remain a near-term headwind." According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders are now pricing in a 58% probability of a rate hike this month. (giulia.petroni@wsj.com)

0732 GMT - Yields on U.K. government bonds, or gilts, rise as oil prices accelerate due to new U.S.-Iran hostilities. The U.S. said it struck three Iranian oil tankers over the weekend, after Iran launched missiles toward two Navy warships. Bond investors are concerned that elevated oil prices could cause higher inflation, raising the risk of the Bank of England increasing interest rates in the coming months. Ten-year gilt yields rise 2.4 basis points to last trade at 5.162%, Tradeweb data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

title: German Industrial Output Fall Primarily Down to Car Production Changes — Market Talk
